title: A monthly child benefit: the American Family Act's new section 24A
parameters: For each child under 18: $300 a month at ages 6 to 17 and $360 under 6 (120%), with $2,400 in a newborn's first month (800%), in 2025 dollars, indexed to prices from 2024 and rounded to $10 (about $340 and $410 a month in 2030 on CBO's prices; project arithmetic). Fully refundable. Replaces the 2025 law's $2,200 credit for children; 17-year-olds, whom the 2025 law leaves out, are covered. Effective for tax year 2030, paid monthly (FAM-1.07). The 2,400-dollar first month is paid in the month after the birth is recorded
current_law: P.L. 119-21: a $2,200 credit a child under 17, indexed after 2025, refundable only to $1,700 and 15% of earnings above $2,500; a work-eligible Social Security number for the child and at least one parent; paid once a year at filing [EV-SEC-001] [EV-SEC-003] [EV-SEC-005] [EV-SEC-006]; no IRS Direct File [EV-SEC-063]

title: The bill's own phase-out, with no $2,200 floor
parameters: The extra amount falls by 5% of modified AGI above $150,000 for joint returns and $112,500 for others, indexed from 2022 and rounded to $5,000 (about $180,000 and $135,000 in 2030), down to $166.67 a month a child ($2,000 a year, not indexed); the rest falls by 5% above $400,000 joint and $300,000 for others, not indexed. A family may use the current or either of the two prior years' income, as the bill allows. *What declining the floor changes:* about 8.8 million children in about 5.4 million families, all above about $210,000 (couples) or $165,000 (others) in 2030, get less than the 2029 law's $2,200 indexed credit would pay them: about $500 a child in 2030, about $1,100 by 2040 as the law's indexed credit grows and the bill's $2,000 does not. The floor would have cost about $4-6 billion a year, about $0.05 trillion over FY2030-39 (project arithmetic, `tools/afa_floor.py`; section 6, part 1). It reaches no poor children: about 5,500 of 9.7 million in the source year

title: Paid to the parent the child lives with
parameters: The payee is the parent or caregiver with whom the child has the same principal home for more than half of the month, as the bill's monthly residence test provides, on that person's attestation. Shared custody of about equal time: the benefit splits evenly. A change of payee when a child moves takes one statement, effective the next month. A dispute goes to a short administrative review by the IRS (FAM-1.10's front doors take the statement), not a tax audit; the payee keeps the payment until the review decides. *Except for safety:* a claimant who states that they left the other parent's home with the child because of abuse becomes the payee from the next month, the other parent bearing the burden of a dispute, and the claimant's address never appears on the other parent's notice (working choice)

title: The $500 credit for other dependents ends, as the bill provides
parameters: The American Family Act ends section 24 for tax years after 2024 (H.R. 2763, sec. 2(c)), and with it the 2025 law's $500 credit for dependents who are not children under 18 (college students, disabled adult children, parents a family supports). The provision follows the bill. Against the 2029 law, families who claim the credit lose up to $500 a dependent, about $5-7 billion a year in all (project arithmetic: about 14.8 million adults claimed as dependents at $500, an upper bound, since the credit is nonrefundable). The plan's other benefits cover most of these groups at larger amounts (the Social Security and SSI changes, the care benefit, the single health plan); college students' costs go to the education dossier (EDU-5). Reinstating the credit stays an option if a gap shows (section 8)

title: SSI extended to Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa
status: decided: Espen, November 12, lead session (DEC entry to come with the booking PR)
parameters: From January 2031 (working choice: a year for SSA to open claims there), SSI's federal benefit and rules, with INC-3.01's and 3.02's limits, apply to bona fide residents of the four territories as in the states; the Northern Mariana Islands already have SSI [EV-SEC-703]. It replaces the Aid to the Aged, Blind, or Disabled program in Puerto Rico, Guam and the Virgin Islands: AABD recipients move to SSI from the territories' records without a new application, new claims are decided under SSI's rules, the AABD part of each territory's grant under section 1108 of the Social Security Act ends at conversion, and a territory may supplement SSI as a state may. Children with disabilities, whom AABD leaves out, are covered. Medicaid follows health's territorial rule (HLT-7.28). Congress may extend SSI this way: *United States v. Vaello Madero* (2022) held that the Constitution does not require it, not that Congress may not. title: Full benefits on time if depletion comes first
parameters: If a trust fund cannot pay scheduled benefits in full before the act's revenue is enough, the general fund lends it the shortfall, so SSA pays full benefits on time; repaid with interest from the act's revenue. Enacted with the act and effective at once; if the act slips past 2031, it moves first as a short bill (section 8). The retirement fund is projected short in the fourth quarter of 2032 [EV-SEC-400]

vehicle.note: Social Security Solvency and Protection Act of 2030

current_law: OASI short in the fourth quarter of 2032, then 78% payable; 75-year gap 4.42% of payroll [EV-SEC-400] [EV-SEC-402]; the law does not say what SSA does at depletion [EV-SEC-412]

title: The floor's non-wage payments never count as income
parameters: , in R1 One section, modeled on 26 U.S.C. 6409: the child benefit, the Climate Dividend, LAB-10's stipends, the plan's refundable credits and the value of free or capped child care are not income, and not resources for 12 months, for any federal or federally funded program. Paid leave and Social Security, the minimum benefit and caregiver credit included, count as the wages they replace
agency: Every program agency; HUD, USDA and HHS issue conforming rules
current_law: Only tax-code refunds and refundable credits are excluded from other programs' income (26 U.S.C. 6409) [EV-SEC-534]; no ceiling on combined phase-out rates

title: A published 65-cent ceiling, met by design rules
parameters: For the household model's typical families (a single parent of two, a married couple with two, a single adult) at 50% to 300% of poverty, the combined rate from every federal layer, taxes included, stays at or below 65 cents per added dollar; housing's 30% rent rule is outside it. *Design rules:* no plan benefit adds a phase-out below 200% of poverty beyond the childless earned income credit's (INC-1.01), which memo 7 counted; INC-5.01; one income finding reused across programs (INC-5.03); benefits held for a set period after a raise. *Monitoring:* the household model publishes the distribution each year; a family type above the ceiling for two years triggers a review by the owning dossiers. No statutory cap and no new calculation for families
agency: Treasury (OTA) publishes, with the household model (`MOD-household`)
current_law: Only tax-code refunds and refundable credits are excluded from other programs' income (26 U.S.C. 6409) [EV-SEC-534]; no ceiling on combined phase-out rates

title: One income finding, reused
status: decided, memo 7 part 2 B's design rules
parameters: A program may rely on another federal program's income determination from the prior year's return or its own records, as HUD and express-lane Medicaid already may; the child benefit's and the credits' finding is the default
